Similar but Not Redundant: Embedding-Gated Refinement for High-Granularity Topic Models

Daniel Denley Affiliation: Strategic Futures Lab, Heriot-Watt University, Edinburgh, United Kingdom Affiliation: STMicroelectronics, Edinburgh, United Kingdom Email: dad2001@hw.ac.uk    Robert L. Nicol Affiliation: STMicroelectronics, Edinburgh, United Kingdom Email: robert.nicol@st.com    Mike J. Chantler Affiliation: Strategic Futures Lab, Heriot-Watt University, Edinburgh, United Kingdom Email: M.J.Chantler@hw.ac.uk
Abstract

High-granularity topic modelling extracts hundreds of niche topics from a corpus, yet this regime is rarely studied and is more commonly framed as a failure mode: "over-clustering," in which coherent themes fragment into redundant subtopics. We argue that this framing conflates genuine redundancy with topics that are semantically similar but meaningfully distinct, and that the central challenge in high-granularity modelling is separating the two. Recent post-hoc refinement methods address topic redundancy through either embedding-based similarity thresholding or LLM-guided merging. We show that neither suffices in high-granularity settings and propose embedding-gated iterative merge (EGIM), a hybrid approach that iteratively generates context-rich topic representations, uses embedding similarity to propose candidate merges across the topic space, then applies LLM judgement to accept only genuinely redundant pairs while preserving niche distinctions. Across two patent corpora and one legal corpus, LLM judgement rejects 83% of embedding-identified candidates as non-redundant. EGIM improves discriminability on merged topics by 25–55% over a prior iterative LLM baseline while better preserving the original topic distribution.

1 Introduction

Standard topic model benchmarks operate at moderate granularity, typically between 20 and 100 topics. Yet a range of downstream text-mining tasks, such as competitive intelligence in patent informatics Tang et al. (2012) and area-of-law mapping in legal corpora Wendel et al. (2022), can benefit from niche topic extraction via high-granularity topic model regimes. When models are pushed to higher topic counts, the result is commonly framed as "over-clustering": outputs that are overly complex and yield many redundant or highly similar topics, reducing topic interpretability and practical usefulness Greene et al. (2014); Meaney et al. (2023); Gan and Qi (2021). We argue that this framing conflates genuinely redundant topics with semantically similar but distinct ones, and that the core challenge in high-granularity topic modelling is developing refinement methods that can distinguish the two.

Topic redundancy is a well-documented issue in topic modelling Greene et al. (2014); O’Callaghan et al. (2015), including with LLM-generated topic descriptors Mu et al. (2024); Singh et al. (2025). Prior work on post-hoc reduction of topic redundancy falls into two broad categories: similarity-threshold methods, which merge topics based on vector distances Grootendorst (2022), and LLM-guided methods, which prompt language models to identify and consolidate redundant topics Janssens et al. (2025); Pham et al. (2024). We show that neither is adequate in high-granularity regimes: threshold methods cannot distinguish genuinely redundant pairs from semantically similar ones, and LLM-guided methods are susceptible to semantic snowballing, in which progressively broader merged labels attract further merges and collapse the topic distribution.

We propose embedding-gated iterative merge (EGIM), a hybrid post-hoc refinement method that uses embedding similarity to select candidate topic pairs, then reduces each decision to a binary merge-or-keep judgment by a single LLM call. Because each call concerns one pair, the prompt can include representative documents from both topics, grounding the decision in corpus evidence rather than label semantics alone. Candidate pairs are selected via k-means sampling across the topic-embedding space rather than by greedy similarity sampling; we show in an ablation that this coverage-based strategy identifies more true duplicates. Because EGIM operates as a merge-keep loop, termination is conditioned on convergence (a fixed number of consecutive iterations without a merge) rather than a predefined target topic count. In practice, merge occurrences decrease steadily across iterations and the method converges naturally.

To evaluate post-hoc refinement in high-granularity regimes, we introduce two diagnostics: topic dispersion, which measures distributional balance and penalises mega-topics more heavily than niche ones, and topic discriminability, which measures how well a topic’s representation aligns with its assigned documents relative to non-assigned documents. Across two patent corpora and a legal corpus, we find that 83% of high-similarity topic pairs are rejected as non-redundant by the LLM. EGIM improves topic discriminability by 25–55% over an iterative LLM baseline while preserving over 94% of original topic dispersion across all three corpora, compared to 34–88% for the baseline.

Our main contributions are:

  • •

    Embedding-gated iterative refinement. We propose EGIM, a hybrid post-hoc refinement algorithm that selects candidate pairs via embedding similarity with coverage-based sampling, then applies LLM judgement grounded in representative documents to merge genuine duplicates whilst preserving semantically similar but distinct topics. The method is convergence-terminated and does not require a predefined target topic count.

  • •

    Evaluation diagnostics for high-granularity refinement. We propose topic dispersion and topic discriminability as diagnostics designed for high topic counts, replacing standard metrics that treat inter-topic similarity as sufficient evidence of redundancy.

2 Related Work

High-Granularity Topic Modeling.

Most topic modeling research evaluates at low to moderate granularity, with topic counts optimized for automated metrics or drawn from standardized ranges on benchmark corpora. Work explicitly targeting high-granularity regimes is typically driven by downstream requirements. Boutaleb et al. (2024) propose BERTrend, a framework for detecting weak thematic signals and emerging trends, built on BERTopic with hyperparameters selected for the explicit purpose of producing fine-grained topics. The FIDELITY framework (Singh et al., 2025) identifies a research gap in topic modeling approaches for high-granularity output and proposes clustering extracted keyphrases to produce fine-grained phrasal topics. Singh et al. (2025) also raise concerns about their post-hoc redundancy method based on cosine similarity, noting it may oversimplify distinctions between closely related topics, and suggest LLM-based merging as a potential remedy.

Post-hoc Topic Refinement.

Existing approaches to post-hoc topic redundancy reduction fall into two broad categories.

Threshold-based strategies consolidate topics by the similarity of their vector representations. BERTopic (Grootendorst, 2022) implements topic reduction via agglomerative clustering over class-based TF-IDF representations. Blair et al. (2020) apply a comparable strategy to aggregated LDA ensembles, merging topics that exceed predefined cosine similarity and Jensen–Shannon divergence thresholds. These methods are efficient but cannot judge whether two similar topics are genuinely redundant or capture meaningful distinctions at fine granularity.

LLM-facilitated methods replace or supplement similarity thresholds with language model judgment. PromptTopic (Wang et al., 2023) includes a topic-collapse stage that uses an LLM to merge overlapping topics based solely on topic names until a target topic count is obtained. TopicGPT (Pham et al., 2024) similarly details a single-step hybrid clean-up stage in which they first identify topic labels above a set threshold (>0.5 cosine similarity) before passing topic lists to an LLM to make merge decisions. Most similar to our work is that of Janssens et al. (2025), who specifically investigates reduction of overlapping topics from base model outputs (BERTopic). Janssens et al. (2025) iteratively utilises an LLM to perform both topic candidate selection and merged topic representation from the current topic representation list, until a desired topic count is reached.

Our work extends this line of research by decoupling candidate selection from merge judgment. Prior LLM-facilitated methods present the model with full or partial topic lists, requiring it to simultaneously identify merge candidates and execute merges. This scales poorly to high-granularity settings, where hundreds of thematically narrow topics exhaust the context window and leave little room for the document-level evidence needed to distinguish genuine redundancy from meaningful specificity. Our method instead uses semantic embeddings for thematically-aware candidate selection, reducing each merge decision to a single topic pair presented alongside representative documents for binary LLM judgment. The topic landscape is then updated and the process repeats, allowing natural convergence rather than reduction to a predefined count. Empirically, we find that the LLM rejects the majority of embedding-selected candidates, particularly in later iterations, demonstrating that similarity-threshold selection alone systematically conflates semantic proximity with genuine redundancy at high granularity.

3 Methodology

3.1 Embedding-Gated Iterative Merge

Given an initial high-granularity topic model with document–topic assignments and a keyword-based topic representation, we first generate contextually rich topic representations by prompting an LLM with each topic’s keywords and representative documents to produce a descriptive label and summary. The refinement algorithm then operates over these LLM-generated representations, iteratively removing redundant topics. The algorithm does not require specifying a target topic count; it terminates when no merge occurs for NN consecutive rounds (patience parameter) or when an LLM call budget is reached. The output is an updated topic set with revised representations and merged assignments.

At each iteration, topic embeddings are recomputed to reflect any merges from the previous round, then clustered into M=max⁡(2,⌊K/s⌋)M{=}\max(2,\lfloor K/s\rfloor) groups via k-means, where KK is the current number of active topics and ss is a target cluster size. This makes MM adaptive: as topics are merged and KK decreases, fewer clusters are formed.

The highest-cosine-similarity unreviewed pair above threshold τ\tau is selected from each cluster, ensuring broad coverage across the embedding space rather than concentrating on a single high-density region. In practice, this yields more successful merges per LLM call than greedy selection over the full space.

Representative documents StS_{t} are selected to balance relevance and diversity via MMR-based selection with quality filtering. When retrieving representative documents, if the topic is a product of prior merges, representative documents are drawn as evenly as possible from each underlying topic to maintain balanced coverage of the merged topic’s thematic scope.

For each candidate pair, we provide the LLM with both topic representations and representative documents and ask it to choose one of two actions:

  • •

    Merge: combine the two topics, producing a new representation and merged assignment set.

  • •

    Keep: leave both topics unchanged when they are similar but represent meaningfully distinct concepts.

The prompts encode a conservative granularity policy that favours Keep when topics address distinct aspects of a shared domain, and Merge only when they describe the same underlying concept; in practice, this policy can be adjusted to reflect application needs. We cache declined pairs (ℰ\mathcal{E}) to avoid repeated judgement calls; since merges produce a new topic, cached entries involving the constituent topics naturally become stale and the new topic is evaluated afresh against its neighbours. Full prompt templates and implementation details are provided in Appendix A and Appendix B.

3.2 Datasets

We evaluate on three corpora from domains where fine-grained thematic distinctions carry practical value: two patent collections obtained via Lens.org11 1 https://www.lens.org/ (Jefferson et al., 2021) and one legal case reports corpus.

  • •

    SPAD Patents (1,102 documents): Patents related to Single-Photon Avalanche Diodes, a niche semiconductor domain.

  • •

    Laser Defense Patents (3,302 documents): Laser technology patents assigned to defense organizations.

  • •

    Legal Case Reports (3,890 documents): Australian Federal Court cases full text dataset (Galgani and Hoffmann, 2010), taken from the UCI Machine Learning Repository 22 2 https://archive.ics.uci.edu/dataset/239/legal+case+reports.

Patents are represented using description section text. Full curation details, including pre-filtering criteria, are provided in Appendix C.

3.3 Experimental Design

We split our evaluation into two stages. Stage A performs a multi-factor calibration sweep to characterize how modeling choices interact in high-granularity topic modeling pipelines. In Stage B, we apply the insights from Stage A to produce high-granularity topic models on our datasets, then isolate the effect of our post-hoc refinement.

Base Topic Model.

We adopt BERTopic (Grootendorst, 2022) as our base topic model to produce initial document–topic assignments and topic representations. BERTopic is representative of the embedding-cluster framework popular in modern topic modeling: documents or document chunks are encoded with a sentence-transformer model, embeddings reduced via UMAP McInnes et al. (2020), clustered with HDBSCAN Campello et al. (2015), and each cluster represented via class-based term frequency–inverse document frequency (c-TF-IDF) keyword extraction.

Stage A: Base Model Configuration Sweep.

Stage A investigates how chunk size and preprocessing interact with granularity in the base BERTopic model. We perform a factorial sweep over corpus ×\times preprocessing ×\times chunk size ×\times KK: three corpora, six preprocessing variants, three chunk sizes {2,5,10}\{2,5,10\} sentences, and five target granularities K∈{20,40,80,160,320}K\in\{20,40,80,160,320\}, yielding 270270 total configurations. As BERTopic’s component models (UMAP and HDBSCAN) are sensitive to the underlying data distribution and desired cluster granularity, we additionally optimize each configuration for 50 trials using Optuna (Akiba et al., 2019), with a composite objective balancing topic quality and cluster validity (Appendix D).

Stage B: Post-hoc Refinement Comparison.

Stage B isolates the effect of refinement by fixing chunk size to 2 sentences and target granularity to K=320K{=}320, guided by Stage A findings (Section 4.3), while retaining all six preprocessing variants across all three corpora to give 18 base topic models. Each refinement method is applied to every base model and compared using dispersion and discriminability as primary diagnostics, targeting the two main failure modes of high-granularity refinement: granularity loss via distribution collapse and non-discriminative topic labels.

3.4 Metrics

Conventional metrics.

We compute NPMI Lau et al. (2014), cvc_{v} Röder et al. (2015), and UMass Mimno et al. (2011) coherence using the Gensim Python library Rehurek and Sojka (2011), as these remain widely adopted automated evaluation metrics for topic models despite known limitations in their alignment with human judgment (Hoyle et al., 2021). All coherence metrics and topic diversity Dieng et al. (2020) are computed over the top-1010 c-TF-IDF keywords per topic. Topic diversity is defined as the proportion of unique words across all topics. Sliding window sizes follow Gensim defaults (110110 for cvc_{v}, 1010 for NPMI). All metrics use the target corpus as the reference text.

LLM-based evaluation.

Following Stammbach et al. (2023), we use an LLM to approximate two standard human evaluation tasks: (i) coherence rating, where the model scores keyword relatedness on a 1–3 scale over the top-10 c-TF-IDF keywords, and (ii) word intrusion, where the model identifies an intruder keyword injected among five topic keywords. Word intrusion was introduced by Chang et al. (2009) as a human evaluation task that measures the semantic coherence of topics, specifically whether the representative words of the topics form a coherent enough group that the intruder word can be identified. Stammbach et al. (2023) show that LLM coherence ratings correlate more strongly with human judgments than conventional automated metrics, and that LLM word-intrusion accuracy approaches that of humans. We use GPT-4o OpenAI et al. (2024) with domain-adapted prompts (Appendix A).

Topic Dispersion.

We quantify resistance to topic-size collapse using the effective number of topics, adapted from the effective number of species in ecology (Jost, 2006), computed as the reciprocal of the Herfindahl–Hirschman Index. Let pkp_{k} be the fraction of documents assigned to topic kk:

Neff=1∑k=1Kpk2N_{\text{eff}}=\frac{1}{\sum_{k=1}^{K}p_{k}^{2}} (1)

To compare models with different KK, we normalize to a 0–1 score:

Dispersion=Neff−1K−1\text{Dispersion}=\frac{N_{\text{eff}}-1}{K-1} (2)

A score of 1 indicates a uniform topic-size distribution; values near 0 indicate collapse into a few dominant topics. The metric is most sensitive to concentration in a few dominant topics and less affected by size variation among smaller ones. We use dispersion as a primary outcome in Stage B to quantify whether refinement induces or prevents collapse.

Topic discriminability.

We measure how well a topic representation distinguishes its assigned documents from the broader corpus. Let rtr_{t} be the embedding of a topic representation (label + summary), and let ede_{d} be the embedding of a document chunk dd under the same embedding model used for clustering. For each topic tt with assigned set DtD_{t}, we compute mean cosine similarity to assigned documents (intra) and to all non-outlier documents not assigned to that topic (inter):

Intra​(t)=1|Dt|​∑d∈Dtcos⁡(rt,ed)\text{Intra}(t)=\frac{1}{|D_{t}|}\sum_{d\in D_{t}}\cos(r_{t},e_{d}) (3)
Inter​(t)=1|D∖Dt|​∑d∉Dtcos⁡(rt,ed)\text{Inter}(t)=\frac{1}{|D\setminus D_{t}|}\sum_{d\notin D_{t}}\cos(r_{t},e_{d}) (4)

and define discriminability as the margin:

Discrim​(t)=Intra​(t)−Inter​(t)\text{Discrim}(t)=\text{Intra}(t)-\text{Inter}(t) (5)

Discriminability is defined over label+summary representations produced during refinement. Since refinement typically merges only a fraction of the total topics, changes are too diluted to detect at the full topic-set level; we therefore report the average over merged topics, where each merged topic’s inter-similarity is computed against all non-outlier documents outside its own assignment set.

4 Experiments

4.1 Experimental Setup

Topic modeling pipeline.

Sentence segmentation is performed using the "Segment Any Text" Python library Frohmann et al. (2024)33 3 https://huggingface.co/segment-any-text/sat-12l-sm for sentence-level chunking. Document chunks are embedded with Qwen3-Embedding-0.6B Zhang et al. (2025)44 4 https://huggingface.co/Qwen/Qwen3-Embedding-0.6B using domain-specific instruction prompts (Appendix A). GPT-4o is used for all LLM components across both stages: representation initialization (from top-10 c-TF-IDF keywords and 5 representative documents), pairwise merge judgments, and evaluation metrics.

Refinement hyperparameters.

For EGIM (Algorithm 1), we set the similarity threshold τ=0.75\tau=0.75, target cluster size s=15s=15, patience N=3N=3, and a maximum budget of 200 LLM calls. Each merge decision includes 5 representative documents per topic.

Preprocessing variants.

Across both stages we evaluate six preprocessing variants: uncleaned text; stopword removal; rule-based cleaning (regex); and three LLM-assisted boilerplate-removal variants. Each LLM-assisted variant clusters sentences in embedding space, samples representative sentences, and uses an LLM to classify clusters as boilerplate for removal. Full definitions and parameters are provided in Appendix E.

4.2 Baseline

We compare EGIM against the iterative LLM-based topic reduction method of Janssens et al. (2025) (hereafter LLM-Iter). At each iteration, LLM-Iter presents the current topic representations to the LLM and prompts it to identify and merge the two most similar topics, repeating until a target count is reached. We use the same topic representation form as EGIM (LLM-generated label+summary) so that differences reflect the method structure rather than the topic representation type. Two key differences between methods remain: (i) EGIM uses embedding similarity to identify candidate pairs rather than relying on the LLM for candidate selection; and (ii) EGIM permits the LLM to decline a merge, whereas LLM-Iter merges unconditionally the candidates identified.

Matched final topic count.

EGIM does not target a specific topic count, instead converging under a fixed budget. For fair comparison, we first run EGIM on each base model to obtain its converged count K′K^{\prime}, then run LLM-Iter to the same K′K^{\prime}, ensuring both methods are evaluated for the same reduction degree.

4.3 Calibration Sweep (Stage A)

Stage A identifies upstream pipeline settings suited to high-granularity BERTopic, producing the base models for Stage B.

Coherence metric reliability.

Conventional coherence metrics show inconsistent behaviour across our corpora. To assess reliability, we correlate each conventional metric with the two LLM-based measures of Stammbach et al. (2023): coherence rating, an extrinsic coherence measure that does not rely on co-occurrence statistics of the underlying corpus, and word-intrusion accuracy, a task-based metric where the model either correctly identifies the intruder word or it does not. UMass correlates consistently with both LLM measures across all three corpora (ρ=0.56\rho=0.56–0.660.66 with intrusion accuracy, p<0.001p<0.001; surviving Bonferroni correction for 18 comparisons). NPMI and cvc_{v} do not: both exhibit sign reversals, correlating positively on laser but negatively or non-significantly on legal (Appendix Table 10). This aligns with prior concerns about the reliability of automated coherence metrics Hoyle et al. (2021).

Granularity selection.

We target K=320K{=}320 to enable the fine-grained topic distinctions required by downstream applications such as competitive intelligence. To verify that quality degrades gracefully at this granularity, we compare across K∈{20,40,80,160,320}K\in\{20,40,80,160,320\} (Table 1). Quality declines gradually overall, with intrusion accuracy at K=320K{=}320 still well above the 17% chance baseline.

Chunk size and preprocessing.

At K=320K{=}320, 2-sentence chunks perform best on two of three corpora (Appendix Table 11); we fix chunk size to 2 sentences for Stage B. The best preprocessing method differs by corpus (Appendix Table 12), so Stage B retains all six variants, yielding 18 base models (3 corpora ×\times 6 methods).

4.4 Post-hoc Refinement Results (Stage B)

Since preprocessing variants within each corpus share underlying documents, we report corpus-level aggregates (n=3n{=}3) and emphasise effect sizes and consistency.

Dispersion.

Both methods perform the same number of merge operations to reach the matched K′K^{\prime} (mean 33). However, LLM-Iter concentrates these into 5.4 distinct target topics on average, whereas EGIM distributes merges across 17.1 distinct targets. Under LLM-Iter, the same dominant topics repeatedly absorb others, a process we refer to as semantic snowballing. Table 2 shows the resulting dispersion gap: LLM-Iter preserves only 34% to 88% of original dispersion, with severe collapse on SPAD, while EGIM maintains above 94%.

Discriminability.

Table 3 reports discriminability on merged topics. EGIM consistently achieves higher scores across all three corpora, with improvements ranging from +25% (LASER) to +55% (SPAD), outperforming in 16 of 18 configurations (5/6 LASER, 5/6 LEGAL, 6/6 SPAD).

Semantic snowballing.

Table 4 illustrates semantic snowballing under LLM-Iter. Six topics covering LIDAR, explosive detection, laser guidance, and wavelength selection are progressively absorbed into a single topic. EGIM evaluated several of the same pairs: LIDAR and LADAR Systems was paired with Weapon-Locating Ladar (similarity 0.796), and Laser Range Finding with Weapon-Locating Ladar. In both cases the LLM declined to merge. Across the full run, all six topics remained separate under EGIM. Further examples appear in Appendix G.4.

Limits of threshold-based merging.

Across all runs, EGIM evaluated 3,491 candidate pairs above the similarity threshold, merging 596 (17%) and declining 2,895 (83%). Figure 1 shows substantial overlap between the similarity distributions of merged and declined pairs (mean 0.846 vs. 0.801), with overall AUC of 0.824 (per-corpus: 0.75 SPAD, 0.80 LEGAL, 0.89 LASER). The optimal threshold under Youden’s J (0.823) catches only 72.7% of true merges while wrongly merging 22.1% of keeps. Raising the threshold to 0.85 reduces false merges to 5.8% but misses 57% of LLM judged duplicates.

Table 5 illustrates this: Contract Interpretation Principles and Statutory Interpretation Principles reach .893 similarity yet describe fundamentally different legal doctrines, while Tax Assessment Objections and Taxation Objection Appeals at .861 are redundant.

Overall model quality.

Across both traditional (cvc_{v}, cn​p​m​ic_{npmi}, diversity) and LLM-evaluated (coherence, intrusion) metrics, all changes remain under 3% for both methods (Appendix G.1). This is expected: refinement affects only merged topics, which constitute roughly 10% of the final topic set on average.

Convergence.

The merge rate declines from approximately 30% in the first three rounds to below 8% after round 8, aggregated over the 18 configurations. Some corpora exhaust the 200-call budget more often (SPAD: 6/6, LEGAL: 5/6, LASER: 2/6), reflecting more judged topic redundancy. Even in budget-limited runs, productive merging is concentrated in early rounds; later calls predominantly result in decline decisions. Convergence across iterations is visualised in Figure 2 (Appendix G.2).

Coverage-based sampling ablation.

To isolate the effect of k-means coverage gating, we compare EGIM against a variant that selects candidate pairs by greedy similarity ranking over the full topic space, holding all other components fixed (single LASER configuration, equal LLM calls). Coverage gating finds 56% more merges (14 vs. 9) at 36% better efficiency (12.6 vs. 19.7 calls per merge). Without coverage gating, candidate selection concentrates on a narrower region of the topic space (53.8% of topics evaluated vs. 62.2%), and individual topics reappear more frequently (max 9 vs. 6 appearances), indicating repeated evaluation of the same neighbourhood rather than exploration of the full thematic space.

Computational cost.

EGIM requires more LLM calls than LLM-Iter (mean 193.9 vs. 66.2, a 2.9×\times increase). This reflects the cost of selectivity: EGIM evaluates candidates that it ultimately declines, whereas LLM-Iter merges unconditionally at each step. In practice the cost is front-loaded, as the majority of productive merges occur in early rounds with a steady decline in valid merges found as iterations progress. A lower budget would capture most of the benefit.

5 Conclusion

We introduce EGIM, a methodology that can be applied to base topic models for topic redundancy removal in high-granularity regimes. Through a series of design decisions we resolve limitations of prior post-hoc refinement strategies that result in incorrect merging and distribution collapse, both leading to reduction in desired granularity. To measure the common failure modes of high-granularity modelling we proposed (i) topic dispersion, a distribution metric that penalises topic collapse, and (ii) topic discriminability, a metric for measuring the distinctiveness of a topic label within a topic model, key for useful high-granularity topic modelling.

Across two patent corpora and a legal corpus, we found that 83% of high-similarity candidate pairs were rejected as non-redundant by LLM judgment, confirming that semantic similarity alone cannot distinguish true duplicates from distinct-but-related topics. EGIM distributed merges across 3.1×3.1{\times} more distinct targets than the iterative LLM baseline, preserving over 94% of original dispersion while improving discriminability on merged topics by 25–55%.

Limitations

Ablation Limitations.

Our study utilised a single embedding model for core topic modelling and topic representation sampling, and a single LLM for both the methodology and evaluation. Whilst we chose a modern instruction-tuned embedding model for our experiments, it would be interesting to investigate how different model sizes and potential domain fine-tuning alter results. In particular, our candidate selection uses Qwen3-Embedding-0.6B; different embedding models may shift the similarity distributions for the merge/keep decisions, and domain-tuned embedding models may better differentiate genuinely duplicate pairs from related-but-distinct ones, potentially decreasing the AUC overlap of merge and keep decisions when applied to specific corpora. The coverage-based sampling ablation was also conducted on a single configuration rather than across all 18, limiting the strength of that finding. Early testing found that local LLM models struggled with producing high-quality topic representations and topic evaluation, however we foresee this limitation dissolving with the current upward performance trend of smaller LLMs.

Evaluation Limitations.

Stage A hinted at an interesting result in conventional coherence metric reliability at high granularity, with UMass maintaining consistent correlation with our LLM human-task proxies. Whilst this may be a result of the structure of the UMass metric (no sliding windows, thus potentially handling rare vocabulary better), we did not feel confident enough with our amount of data to make definitive claims. In addition, whilst topic discriminability and topic dispersion worked well to measure our targeted failure modes, we saw little change in model-wide metrics after post-hoc refinement under either method. We attribute this to the relatively low proportion of topics that get altered in our high-granularity regime, but investigating how these metrics change with more aggressive reduction (lowering the similarity threshold, increasing the LLM call budget, or altering the merge prompt to favour merge decisions more readily) would be an interesting direction.

Corpora Limitations.

Both our embedding model and LLM are capable of multilingual processing, however all three corpora were constrained to English. It would be a useful investigation to see how a multilingual dataset alters the methodology’s decisions in how topics are merged and represented. In addition, we chose to use three specialised corpora over traditional topic model benchmark corpora. This decision was made because our corpora represent real-world targets for high-granularity regimes that could provide valuable input to downstream use cases; however, a trade-off in cross-work comparison was made, and future investigation into post-hoc refinement for high-granularity regimes should consider including standard benchmarks.

Closed-Source Models.

Our methodology and LLM-based evaluation both rely on OpenAI closed-source models, raising reproducibility concerns: model versioning means our exact results may not be replicable if the underlying model is updated or deprecated, and API costs present a barrier to replication. Whilst we found early on that local models gave inferior results for both topic representation and merge judgment, a systematic comparison of local versus closed-source performance would strengthen reproducibility and help establish the minimum model capability required for effective merge decisions.

Appendix A Prompts

All prompts used in the core pipeline are provided here. Preprocessing-specific prompts are provided in Appendix E. Bracketed placeholders (e.g., [DOCUMENT]) indicate dynamically substituted content. The topic labelling and merge/keep prompts (Prompts A.2–A.3) include a corpus-specific context line as the opening sentence of the system message; the three corpora variants are shown in Table 6. Evaluation prompts for LLM coherence rating and word intrusion detection follow the protocol of Stammbach et al. (2023) with similar domain context.

The placeholder [DOMAIN FOCUS TERM] is substituted with “technical focus” for patent corpora and “legal subject matter” for the legal corpus. [DOMAIN TERM] is substituted with “technology” or “legal concept” respectively.

A.1 Embedding Instruction

Document chunks are embedded using Qwen3-Embedding-0.6B with the task instruction shown in Prompt A.1.

{prompt}

A.2 Initial Topic Representation

After BERTopic produces initial document–topic assignments and c-TF-IDF keyword representations, we generate a descriptive label and summary for each topic. The system message (Prompt A.2) defines output requirements; the user message (Prompt A.2) provides the top-10 c-TF-IDF keywords and up to 10 representative documents selected via MMR-based sampling (Appendix B). Representative documents are truncated to 800 characters each.

A.3 Merge/Keep Judgment

For each candidate pair identified by embedding similarity, the LLM receives both topic representations and their representative documents (Prompt A.3) and makes a binary merge-or-keep decision. Up to 5 representative documents per topic are included, truncated to 200 characters each.

{prompt*}

Merge/keep judgment prompt. The LLM decides whether two candidate topics should be merged or kept separate based on their labels, summaries, and representative documents.

Domain-specific guidance is injected for merge and keep decisions. Table 7 shows an example for the LASER corpus; equivalent guidance is defined for SPAD and LEGAL corpora with domain-appropriate terminology.

Appendix B EGIM Implementation Details

This appendix item describes implementation details of the EGIM refinement loop not covered by the pseudocode in Section 3.1.

B.1 Representative Document Selection

Each topic’s representative text chunks are selected from the chunks assigned to that cluster by HDBSCAN. Three progressively filtered candidate sets are constructed:

Probability-gated set (CpC_{p}).

Text chunks whose HDBSCAN cluster-assignment probability falls in the top 20% quantile for the topic.

Quality-gated set (Cq⊆CpC_{q}\subseteq C_{p}).

Chunks from CpC_{p} satisfying three criteria: (i) minimum length of 350 characters, (ii) at least 5% of tokens match the topic’s top c-TF-IDF keywords, and (iii) stopword density does not exceed 40%.

Diversity-sampled set (Cd⊆CqC_{d}\subseteq C_{q}).

Chunks selected from CqC_{q} via Maximal Marginal Relevance (λ=0.7\lambda{=}0.7 relevance, 0.30.3 diversity penalty). The first chunk is the one closest to the CqC_{q} centroid; subsequent chunks maximise the MMR score.

Selection process.

The target count is 10 chunks for initial labelling and 5 for merge/keep judgments. CdC_{d} forms the core of the representative set. If CqC_{q} is empty, CdC_{d} is sampled from CpC_{p} instead; if CpC_{p} is also empty, all cluster-assigned chunks are used. After MMR sampling, if fewer than the target count have been selected (i.e. the sampled set was smaller than the target), remaining slots are filled from all cluster-assigned chunks ranked by assignment probability. This ensures the LLM always receives sufficient context even for small clusters.

B.2 Post-Merge Updates

When the LLM selects merge, three updates are applied to the surviving topic before the next round begins:

  1. 1.

    Document pooling. Representative documents from both constituent topics are combined via round-robin interleaving and capped at 10. Since each list may itself be the product of earlier merges, this maintains thematic coverage across all constituent topics.

  2. 2.

    Re-embedding. The merged label and summary are re-embedded with Qwen3-Embedding-0.6B so that subsequent similarity computations reflect the updated representation.

  3. 3.

    Cache invalidation. All reviewed-pair entries involving either constituent topic ID are cleared, since the surviving topic’s representation has changed and prior keep decisions may no longer hold.

Appendix C Dataset Curation

This appendix documents the retrieval and filtering steps applied to each corpus. All patent data were obtained from Lens.org (Jefferson et al., 2021).

C.1 SPAD Patent Corpus

Patents were retrieved by CPC classification code, targeting single-photon avalanche diode and related photodetector array technologies. The inclusion codes were H01L27/146* (photodiode arrays), H10F30/225* (avalanche photodiodes, reclassified), and H01L31/107* (avalanche photodiodes, legacy). Documents matching any of the following codes were excluded to remove unrelated technologies sharing classification overlap: G01S13/93*, A47L9/28*, H04N5/232, E05D15*, H01L27/32*, and G02F1/1335. Only English-language granted patents and patent applications published from January 2000 onward were included. Patent family deduplication was applied. The search was executed in October 2024, yielding 1,102 documents. Each patent is represented by its description section text.

C.2 Laser Defense Patent Corpus

This corpus was constructed through per-assignee searches for defense and aerospace organisations including: BAE Systems, Elbit Systems, Israel Aerospace Industries (IAI/Elta), L3Harris, Lockheed Martin, MBDA, Northrop Grumman, Rafael Advanced Defense Systems, Rheinmetall, RTX (Raytheon), and Thales. For each organisation, English-language patents were retrieved where the applicant or owner name matched known variants of the company name and at least one of the title, abstract, or claims fields contained one or more of the following keywords: laser*, LIDAR, "directed energy", DIRCM, "optical parametric*", "stimulated emission*", "beam director*", and "target illuminator*". No date restriction was applied. Patent family deduplication was applied. The final corpus contains 3,302 documents. Patents are represented by their description section text.

C.3 Legal Corpora

The legal corpus consists of 3,890 case reports from the Federal Court of Australia, sourced from AustLII and distributed via the UCI Machine Learning Repository (Galgani and Hoffmann, 2010). The dataset comprises all available cases from 2006–2009. Each case is represented by its full text.

Appendix D Optimisation Details

D.1 Constrained Objective

We constrain the optimisation to prioritise feasibility: the TPE sampler must first find configurations that produce at least KtargetK_{\text{target}} topics before it can meaningfully optimise for quality. Trials where ntopics<Ktargetn_{\text{topics}}<K_{\text{target}} are marked infeasible via a normalised violation score v=max⁡(0,(Ktarget−ntopics)/Ktarget)v=\max(0,\;(K_{\text{target}}-n_{\text{topics}})/K_{\text{target}}). Trials producing fewer than 2 topics or fewer than 100 non-outlier documents are pruned outright as degenerate.

Among feasible trials, the sampler maximises an equally weighted composite of four components: CvC_{v} coherence, topic diversity, topic dispersion, and noise score (1−routlier1-r_{\text{outlier}}).

D.2 Hyperparameter Search Space

Table 8 lists the tuned hyperparameters.

D.3 Optuna Configuration

We use the TPE sampler with the constraint mechanism described above. Each experiment runs 50 trials across target topic counts K∈{20,40,80,160,320}K\in\{20,40,80,160,320\}. Dimensionality reduction and clustering both use RAPIDS-accelerated GPU implementations (cuML UMAP and HDBSCAN). Random seeds are fixed at 42 throughout.

Appendix E Preprocessing Definitions

All six preprocessing variants are applied before embedding and clustering. We tested how removing irrelevant text (boilerplate) before running our topic modelling pipeline would interact with topic model performance and desired granularity.

Variant 1: Uncleaned.

Raw text with no filtering. Serves as the baseline.

Variant 2: Stopword removal.

Standard NLTK English stopwords, in addition to corpus-specific stopwords (tokens appearing in ≥ 70%{\geq}\,70\% of documents) are removed at the token level. This tests whether token-level pre-embedding cleaning can improve subsequent text clustering and thus topic modelling output.

Variant 3: Rule-based.

Domain-specific regex patterns flag entire sentences as noise. For patents, six pattern groups target: section headings (“field of the invention”, “background of the disclosure”), filing metadata (“claims the benefit of”, “continuation of”, “PCT application”), figure and table references (“Fig. 3”, “as illustrated in”), bare specifications without context (“operating temperature”, “frequency … GHz”), generic computing scaffolding (“a processor”, “computer-readable medium”), and claim-style fragments (“the method comprises”, “the apparatus of”). For legal documents, patterns target procedural text (“appeal dismissed”, “hearing date”), case citation references (“see … v.”, “in re”), and structural headings. Sentences shorter than 20 characters or 4 tokens are also removed.

Variants 4–6: LLM-assisted semantic cleaning.

These three variants share a common pipeline but differ in the embedding model or instruction used for the initial sentence clustering step for cleaning (not the chunk-level clustering that precedes topic modelling). The pipeline proceeds as follows:

  1. 1.

    Embed all sentences in the corpus using the variant-specific model and instruction (Table 9).

  2. 2.

    Reduce dimensionality with UMAP (nneighbors=15n_{\text{neighbors}}\!=\!15, ncomponents=30n_{\text{components}}\!=\!30, min_dist=0.1\texttt{min\_dist}\!=\!0.1).

  3. 3.

    Cluster the reduced embeddings with KK-Means, where K=clamp​(⌊N/500⌋, 50, 1000)K=\text{clamp}(\lfloor N/500\rfloor,\;50,\;1000) and NN is the total sentence count.

  4. 4.

    Sample 10 diverse sentences per cluster via farthest-first traversal in embedding space.

  5. 5.

    Classify each cluster by prompting a local Gemma 3 27B55 5 Gemma Team et al. (2025); https://ollama.com/library/gemma3:27b. instance with the sampled sentences. For patents the model assigns one of five categories: specific_technique, generic_capability, pure_specification, legal_boilerplate, or administrative. For legal documents: legal_reasoning, factual_interpretation, statutory_reference, administrative_procedural, or structural_transition.

  6. 6.

    Filter: only sentences belonging to clusters labelled specific_technique (patents) or legal_reasoning (legal) are retained.

The three variants differ solely in how sentences are embedded before clustering, which changes which sentences end up co-clustered and therefore which clusters the LLM sees:

Variant 4, labelled LLM (GTE), uses a general-purpose encoder with no task instruction. Variants 5 and 6 use the same embedding model employed in the main pipeline. Variant 5, labelled LLM (noise), uses a task instruction that attempts to focus the encoding on textual noise rather than signal. Variant 6, labelled LLM (signal), uses the same task instruction employed for topic modelling embeddings in the main pipeline, focusing on substantive content.

Appendix G Stage B Supplementary Results

G.1 Full Model Quality

Table 13 reports all quality metrics across methods and corpora. All grand-mean changes remain within ±\pm3% of the original model, confirming that refinement does not degrade overall topic quality.

G.2 Convergence Behaviour

Figure 2 shows merge and decline decisions across refinement rounds. The merge rate declines from approximately 30% in the first three rounds to below 8% after round 8, confirming that the algorithm converges toward a stable topic set. Corpora with denser similarity structure exhaust the 200-call budget more often (SPAD: 6/6, LEGAL: 5/6, LASER: 2/6), reflecting a larger pool of candidate pairs.

G.3 Per-Corpus Similarity Distributions

The aggregate AUC of 0.824 reported in Section 4.4 masks substantial corpus-level variation. Figure 3 shows that LASER’s sparser topic space produces well-separated merge and decline distributions, while SPAD’s smaller corpus yields inherently more similar topics, compressing both distributions into a narrower similarity band. This confirms that similarity alone is insufficient for merge decisions, particularly in dense corpora.

G.4 Semantic Snowballing Examples

Figures 4–6 show snowball chains observed under LLM-Iter, where successive merges broaden a topic until it absorbs unrelated neighbours. Tables 14–16 show EGIM’s decisions on the same topics.
